lead: An activity is one screen of an Android app: a login form, a list of trains, a single ticket. The user jumps between screens and rotates the phone, and Android must free memory, save battery and let other apps come forward. So the system creates and destroys activity objects itself and calls a fixed order of methods, the life cycle, as the screen becomes visible, gets covered and disappears. Knowing that order tells you where to build the screen, where to start and stop the camera, and where to save a half-typed form.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.3 for the Activity class, the manifest entry and setContentView, and Chapter 2.1 for why Android must reclaim memory from apps it cannot see.

blocks.text: An activity is one screen with one job. Each screen is a Java class that extends Activity (or AppCompatActivity) and calls setContentView to attach an XML layout.
Android cannot start a class it does not know about, so every activity is declared in AndroidManifest.xml:

The MAIN action with the LAUNCHER category marks the screen the app icon opens. Other activities are listed with only android:name. A class missing from the manifest throws ActivityNotFoundException when you try to open it. Chapter 2.5 shows how one activity names another.

While the object lives, Android tracks four states: created (object exists, not visible), started (visible, not in front), resumed (visible, in front, receives touches) and destroyed (object gone). A stopped activity is back in the created state. Visible and foreground are not the same: onStart makes the screen visible, onResume puts it in front. A dialog-style activity on top leaves your activity visible but paused — you can see it, you cannot touch it.
Activities the user opens sit on a back stack inside a task. Pressing Back pops the top activity and returns to the one below.
Android calls these methods, called callbacks, in a fixed order. Override only the ones you need, and always call super first.

items: onCreate(Bundle savedInstanceState) — runs once per instance. Attach the layout, create objects, wire listeners. Keep it fast.
onResume() — the activity is in front and has focus. Start the camera preview, sensor listeners, animations.

onPause() — the activity loses the foreground, because another screen is coming forward or the user pressed Home. Stop animations and release the camera. Be quick: the next activity's onResume waits for your onPause to return.
onStop() — the activity is no longer visible. Release heavy things such as a database cursor or a GPS listener.
onDestroy() — the instance is about to go: rotation, Back, or the system finishing it.
onRestart() — a stopped activity is coming back; it runs before onStart.

blocks.text: To read the order on a real phone, put Log.d("LC", "onCreate") at the top of each override and filter Logcat by the tag LC. The messages appear in the order the callbacks ran, with a timestamp on each line.

When the phone rotates, Android by default throws the activity away and builds a new one, because the new orientation may need a different layout file (Unit 3, screen components and layouts). For a rotation while the activity is resumed the order is onPause, onStop, onDestroy, then onCreate, onStart, onResume on the fresh object. Fields are not copied: an int counter holding 7 comes back as 0.

Carry small state in a Bundle, a key-value store of ints, strings and small objects. onSaveInstanceState(Bundle outState) runs after onPause and before onStop. onCreate receives the same Bundle as savedInstanceState, which is null on a fresh launch.

blocks.code:
onSaveInstanceState(Bundle out):
    super.onSaveInstanceState(out)
    out.putInt("count", count)

onCreate(Bundle saved):
    super.onCreate(saved)
    setContentView(R.layout.activity_main)
    if saved != null:
        count = saved.getInt("count", 0)

blocks.text: A Bundle suits a few hundred bytes. Five thousand rows belong in a file or SQLite (Unit 4). And onDestroy is not guaranteed: when RAM runs low the system may kill the whole process after onStop without calling onDestroy, so save what matters in onPause or onSaveInstanceState.

figure.caption: The activity travels down the callbacks as it leaves the screen and climbs back through onRestart when the user returns. The highlighted box is the resumed state, the only one that receives touches.

spec.aria: A flow of activity callbacks from onCreate down to onDestroy, with a dashed return path from onStop back to onStart through onRestart.

examples.question: An activity logs every callback with Log.d("LC", name). Write the exact log lines in order, and the number of lines, for each action: (a) launch the app from the app drawer, (b) press Home, (c) reopen the app from the recents list, (d) press Back. Then (e) rotate the phone while the activity is resumed. Also state what an int field holding count = 7 shows after that rotation.
steps: (a) Launch: the instance is created, becomes visible, comes to the front. Lines: onCreate, onStart, onResume. That is 3 lines.
(b) Home: the activity is fully hidden behind the launcher. Lines: onPause, onStop. That is 2 lines. A paused-only step would need something that is still visible, such as a dialog.
(c) Recents: a stopped activity returns through onRestart before it is started again. Lines: onRestart, onStart, onResume. That is 3 lines.
(d) Back: the activity leaves the back stack for good. Lines: onPause, onStop, onDestroy. That is 3 lines.
(e) Rotation while resumed: the old instance is destroyed and a new one is created. Lines: onPause, onStop, onDestroy, then onCreate, onStart, onResume. That is 6 lines.

The field count is an ordinary int inside the destroyed object, so the new object starts with count = 0. Saving it with out.putInt("count", count) in onSaveInstanceState and reading it back from savedInstanceState in onCreate brings back 7.
examples.answer: The orders are (a) onCreate, onStart, onResume; (b) onPause, onStop; (c) onRestart, onStart, onResume; (d) onPause, onStop, onDestroy; (e) onPause, onStop, onDestroy, onCreate, onStart, onResume — 17 log lines in all, and the counter reads 0 unless it was saved in a Bundle.
examples.check:
a = ["onCreate", "onStart", "onResume"]
b = ["onPause", "onStop"]
c = ["onRestart", "onStart", "onResume"]
d = ["onPause", "onStop", "onDestroy"]
e = ["onPause", "onStop", "onDestroy", "onCreate", "onStart", "onResume"]
for seq in (a, b, c, d, e):
    print(len(seq))
print(len(a) + len(b) + len(c) + len(d) + len(e))

traps: Saying onPause means the activity is destroyed. It is still alive, and it may still be visible under a dialog; only onStop says it is hidden.
Assuming onDestroy always runs. When the system is short of memory it can kill the process after onStop without any callback, so onDestroy is not a safe place to save data.
Thinking rotation calls onRestart. It does not: the instance is new, so onCreate runs, not onRestart.
Expecting onSaveInstanceState to run when the user presses Back. It does not, because that activity is finishing and its state will never be restored.
Mixing up visible and foreground. onStart gives visibility, onResume gives the foreground; a started-but-not-resumed activity is visible but gets no touches.

quiz.q: Name the seven life cycle callbacks in the order a fresh launch followed by a Back press produces them.
quiz.a: onCreate, onStart, onResume, onPause, onStop, onDestroy. onRestart is the seventh callback but it does not run in this sequence.

quiz.q: Why does Android destroy and recreate an activity when the phone rotates?
quiz.a: The new orientation may need a different layout, for example a layout-land file, and the activity may need different resources and a different screen size. Recreating from scratch is the simple way to pick them up; state must then be carried in a Bundle.

quiz.q: Activity A is resumed. The user opens activity B, then presses Back. List the callbacks of A and of B in order.
quiz.a: Opening B: A onPause, then B onCreate, onStart, onResume, then A onStop. Back: B onPause, onStop, onDestroy, then A onRestart, onStart, onResume.

quiz.q: In which callback do you release the camera and stop a running animation, and why there?
quiz.a: In onPause. The activity is losing the foreground, the camera must be free for the next screen, and onPause must return quickly because the next activity's onResume waits for it.

quiz.q: A developer saves a half-typed form in onDestroy and users report lost text. Explain the cause and the fix.
quiz.a: onDestroy is not guaranteed: the system may kill the process after onStop when memory is low, so the save never runs. Move the save to onPause or onSaveInstanceState, which always run before the activity can be hidden or killed.

quiz.q: A paused activity is still visible but does not respond to touches. Explain using onStart and onResume.
quiz.a: It has passed onStart, so the system is still drawing it, but it has passed onPause, so it lost the foreground and the input focus to the activity in front. Only a resumed activity receives touches.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a task and the back stack?
quiz.a: A task is the group of activities the user thinks of as one app session; the back stack is the ordered list of activities inside it, which Back pops one at a time.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real apps rarely override seven callbacks by hand; they use lifecycle-aware components such as ViewModel and LiveData, which survive rotation so the counter never needs a Bundle. Process death is tested with the developer option 'Don't keep activities', which destroys every activity as soon as it is hidden. Modern code bases also add Jetpack Compose, where the same states exist but the callbacks are replaced by effects and rememberSaveable. Search for 'Android lifecycle-aware components' and 'SavedStateHandle' to go further.
